Vulture Rescue

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In the wake of one of Southern Africa’s worst wildlife poisoning events, a coalition of conservationists, veterinarians, rangers, and pilots unite in a race against time to rescue and rehabilitate e

Summary:
In May 2025, Kruger National Park faced one of its gravest wildlife crises: a mass poisoning event that claimed 123 vultures, including 20 Cape Vultures—an endangered species. Poachers had laced an elephant carcass with highly toxic agrochemicals to harvest body parts for the illegal wildlife trade, leading to this devastating loss .
Amidst this tragedy, a beacon of hope emerged. A rapid response team comprising SANParks rangers, the Endangered Wildlife Trust (EWT), veterinary experts, and aerial support units mobilized swiftly. Their coordinated efforts led to the rescue of 84 vultures, including Cape, White-backed, and Hooded Vultures. Utilizing emergency treatments like atropine, activated charcoal, and fluid therapy, and transporting the birds via specialized vulture ambulances and helicopters, the team achieved a remarkable 96% survival rate among the rescued birds .
This incident underscores the escalating threat of poison poaching in Southern Africa, where vultures are deliberately targeted to prevent them from revealing poaching activities. The loss of these scavengers disrupts ecosystems, as vultures play a crucial role in disposing of carcasses and preventing disease spread .
The successful rescue operation highlights the power of collaboration among conservationists, veterinarians, and park authorities.




Carte Blanche Insert Treatment:

Tonight, on Carte Blanche…
In the wake of one of Southern Africa’s worst wildlife poisoning events, a coalition of conservationists, veterinarians, rangers, and pilots unite in a race against time to rescue and rehabilitate endangered vultures—highlighting the power of collaboration in combating a growing ecological crisis.

Segment Overview
Opening Scene:
• Aerial shots of Kruger National Park's vast landscapes.
• Voiceover introduces the significance of vultures in the ecosystem and the alarming rise in wildlife poisoning incidents.
Act 1: The Discovery
• Detail the detection of the poisoning event on May 6, 2025, by the Endangered Wildlife Trust’s (EWT) poison detection system, which monitors for unusual behavior.
• First responders from SANParks and EWT arrive at the Mahlangeni Section, finding 116 vultures dead and others in distress near a poisoned elephant carcass.
• Interviews with rangers and EWT officials recounting the initial response and emotional impact.
Act 2: The Rescue Operation
• Chronicle the rapid mobilization of individuals from various organizations, including SANParks, EWT, Moholoholo Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre, Briner Veterinary Services, and Wildscapes Veterinary Services.
• Highlight the unprecedented use of SANParks helicopters to airlift 39 vultures to the SANParks K9 facility in Phalaborwa, while 45 were transported via EWT’s specialized vulture ambulance.
• Behind-the-scenes footage / pictures of the rescue efforts, showcasing the coordination and urgency. ( if any are available)
Act 3: Rehabilitation and Recovery
• Inside look at the rehabilitation process at Moholoholo Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre, where teams worked tirelessly to stabilize and care for the vultures.
• Interviews with a veterinarian discussing treatment protocols and the challenges faced.
• Update on the current status of the surviving vultures, those that havee been released and plans for release back into the wild. (which we will film)
Act 4: The Broader Crisis
• Examination of the increasing trend of wildlife poisoning in Southern Africa, with poachers using agricultural toxins to target high-value species like vultures and lions for the illegal wildlife trade.
• Discussion on the ecological impact of such poisonings and the importance of vultures in maintaining healthy ecosystems.
• Insights into the collaborative efforts between SANParks, EWT, and other organizations to combat this growing threat.
Closing Scene:
• Footage of rehabilitated vultures being released back into the wild.
• Reflections from team members on the significance of the rescue operation and the ongoing fight against wildlife poisoning.
• Call to action for continued support and awareness to protect these vital scavengers and the broader ecosystem.

Key Interviewees
• SANParks & EWT rangers/officials involved in the initial response.
• EWT officials overseeing the "Eye in the Sky" system.
• Veterinarian from Moholoholo Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre, Briner Veterinary Services, and Wildscapes Veterinary Services.
• Pilots who facilitated the airlifts.
• Conservation experts discussing the broader implications of wildlife poisoning. ( These can be someone for EWT)

Visual Elements
• Drone footage of Kruger National Park and the rescue operation.
• Close-up shots of vultures during rehabilitation.
• illustrating the "Eye in the Sky" detection system and the spread of poisoning incidents.
• Archival footage of previous wildlife poisoning events for context.

Narrative Tone
• Informative and urgent, emphasizing the severity of the crisis.
• Hopeful and inspiring, showcasing the successful collaboration and resilience of the teams involved.
• Empathetic, highlighting the emotional toll on those working to save the vultures.

Objective
To inform viewers about the critical issue of wildlife poisoning in Southern Africa, demonstrate the power of collaborative conservation efforts, and inspire action to protect endangered species and preserve ecological balance.

Script:


(Erin) The Kruger. Covering over two million hectares and spanning two provinces, it’s one of the world’s biggest national parks. A critical stronghold for conservation.



(Erin) But it's under siege from poachers who sometimes use deadly poisons – not bullets – to kill.



(Gareth) There were just bodies everywhere. There were over a hundred dead birds in the immediate vicinity around the actual carcass.



(Cell phone Subtitles) This is what the product of savagery, poisoning is.



(Erin) After the discovery of what was described as a “crime scene” in the heart of the Kruger, we follow a team of dedicated conservationists fighting for the survival of a threatened species.



(Jessica) So, the birds, they're falling all over the place. They're flailing; they're terrified.



(Erin) It’s a story that takes us from the bush into the underbelly of the urban trade in exotic animals.



(Undercover footage subtitles) I can sell you the whole vulture for R5000.



(Erin) Back to the bush and a sign that all is not lost.



(Gareth) Four, three, two, one.



(Erin) It’s early Saturday morning, and I’m with veteran SANParks rangers Andrew and Karien Desmet. Both have spent over two decades working in the Kruger.



(Erin) An elephant carcass has been discovered nearby and we're heading to the scene.



(Andrew) Driving here, and we see vultures like that, we're like, “There is something here.”



(Erin) Out here, death doesn't announce itself – vultures do. And they're already circling.



(Andrew) What we've noticed is, as we were approaching the site, the vultures are all flying around and they're in the trees. But they're not going down onto the carcass. And that could tell us that perhaps there's a predator on the carcass. And we'll just walk slowly, listen. And then, if something happens, we're going to stand still. We're not just going to run.



(Erin) It's a young elephant bull, dead a few days ago.



(Erin) And definitely not poisoned?



(Andrew) No.



(Erin) How can you tell?



(Andrew) Say we’re coming to a poisoning scene, we’d see dead flies. Then we’d know this is a poisoned carcass.



(Erin) Poachers are increasingly using highly toxic agrochemical pesticides to target predators and scavengers, especially vultures.



(Erin) More and more rangers in the greater Kruger National Park are finding carcasses laced with poison, and its remains like this are putting the vulture population in danger.



(Erin) Last month, the park's Mahlangeni Section in northern Limpopo was the site of one of Southern Africa's deadliest wildlife poisonings.



(Erin) Andrew Desmet discovered the scene from a chopper.



(Andrew) There was quite a lot of the elephant that was gone.



(Erin) Andrew, you were on site on the sixth of May. Can you tell us about the sequence of events for you that morning?



(Andrew) We were monitoring the movement of these vultures and we saw something was developing there. And then, I think it was about half-past eight, nine o'clock at night – we just got a mortality alert on, I think, two of the tags.



(Erin) The alert system, developed by the Endangered Wildlife Trust, involves fitting vultures with tags that send signals if they stop moving.



(Andrew) I got airborne. I flew straight to that position. I could see dead vultures. Then I saw an elephant carcass and I can see a lot of live birds. And I could see straight away this was going to be a massive operation and I straight away started communicating with our group.



(Erin) On the ground, field officer for the Endangered Wildlife Trust, Kyle Walker encountered a gruesome scene.



(Erin) When does it occur to you that this is an environmental crime scene?



(Kyle) Almost immediately. I do remember having to step between birds. There's birds everywhere, and you have to watch your step as you walk around, and found the next one, the next one. Each bush we were looking under, we were finding injured birds and trying to treat as quickly as possible.



(Cell phone) This one has obviously died, unfortunately.



(Erin) One hundred and twenty-two vultures lay dead, poisoned. They included endangered White-backed, Cape and Lappet-faced species.



(Erin) Miraculously, some survived.



(Kyle) Once you treat them, they do perk up a lot. So, the challenge became trying to keep the vultures with you, not letting them escape or fly off. Because they will struggle over the next few days and likely die.



(Cell phone Subtitles) This one has just died. No, he’s still alive.



(Erin) The clock was ticking. Saving the survivors demanded an unprecedented, coordinated effort. Over 20 personnel from conservation, veterinary and enforcement teams launched the Kruger's most extensive wildlife rescue response ever.



(Jessica) A lot of them were critically ill. The poison affects the nervous system in particular. So, the birds have severely compromised breathing.



(Erin) Veterinarian, Jessica Briner had to act fast.



(Erin) What do you remember from when your boots were on the ground, on site?



(Jessica) The numbers are in their hundreds. So, when we arrived, it was carnage because there were already so many birds deceased. There were already 123 by the time I got there.



(Erin) What were you doing to help the birds?



(Jessica) The main thing is to get the antidote in. The drug that we use is called Atropine. Food that is still in the crop needs to be removed, and the more fluids we can give them, the better the body can flush those poisons out.



(Erin) Ninety-four vultures were either airlifted or moved by specialised ambulances for intensive care and monitoring. Gareth Tate, from The Endangered Wildlife Trust, oversaw this crucial operation.



(Gareth) It really was just incredible and inspiring to see how this all came together and is testament to all the work that we've put in to get to this kind of world-class reaction unit. Our Vulture Ambulance can hold 40 birds. I think we managed to double that and even fill our canopies of our vehicles up with birds.



(Cell phone Subtitles) Every single crate’s got two birds, crates scattered everywhere.



(Gareth) It’s so overwhelming. Obviously, it's tragic to see those birds in pain, so it was really something.



(Erin) In the past decade, populations of some vulture species have dropped by an astronomical 80%. Many are poisoned by poachers to either avoid detection or losing snared animals. Some, though, are killed for the muthi trade.



(Gareth) We've seen cases of vultures, the heads and body parts removed, sometimes the entire carcass for the trade and use in traditional medicine. What we understand is that they are used for improving luck. We see it linked to gambling syndicates. So, it improves a guy’s chances of winning a gambling bet or whatever. Even individuals playing lottery are prescribed these vulture body parts, in particular the brain.



(Erin) It’s ironic that consuming vultures in this way could be very unlucky.



(Gareth) Often these vulture body parts are still laced with highly toxic poison, which has a human health concern.



(Erin) From the scrub and savannah of the Kruger, we venture back into the city.



(Erin) Joburg is home to at least two markets where the ingredients for muthi are openly sold.



(Cell phone Subtitles) You can only get parts, not the whole thing.



(Erin) Our team filmed undercover at two of them: the KwaMai-Mai and Faraday markets.



(Cell phone Subtitles) A small piece goes for R150.



(Erin) It didn't take long to find what we were looking for.



(Cell phone Subtitles) I can’t give you the whole thing, just take a piece.



(Erin) The body parts of a variety of vultures were on sale. We were even offered the full carcass of a critically endangered White-backed vulture.



(Cell phone Subtitles) I can sell you a whole vulture for R5000. The head is R2000.



(Erin) Spending a few hours in these markets reveals the extent of the challenge facing conservationists. Given the demand, it’s unlikely the mass killing in May will be the last of its kind.



(Erin) But at a facility just outside Kruger, the same conservationists were preparing for the final chapter in a good news story.



(Erin) At the Moholoholo Wildlife Rehab Centre in Hoedspruit, most of the rescued vultures had been treated and released. But several others, after a slower recovery, are only now ready for their return to the wild.



(Nicky) And then I will put a drop in his eye. There we go. This is antibiotic eye drops.



(Erin) Nicky Rappo is a veterinary nurse.



(Erin) Can you tell me about what rehabilitation you've been doing with the vultures?



(Nicky) When they come in, we tube them. So, we give them fluids, lots and lots of fluids. So, basically, what you want to do is flush the poison out of their system and, from there, they get better. So, you start giving them food. Once they're eating well, we can put them outside as well.



(Erin) For some of Nicky’s patients, today is a big day.



(Erin) In these ten crates are some of the remaining vultures from the rescue in May. But before they go into the wild, they’ll need to be fitted with tracking devices. And if some of the sounds we’ve heard are anything to go by, some of them are very ready to be set free.



(Erin) Before they are released, they need to be marked and fitted with these special backpacks.



(Gareth) This is the Earth Ranger software where we are able to monitor our animals, our tracked animals, at almost near-real time. We can see exactly where these birds have travelled. These provide really important insight into where these birds go and where they encounter threats in the landscape and, of course, monitor the post-rehab success.



(Erin) That's it. Ten vultures in two bakkies, and we are off.



(Erin) Finally, it's time for them to take to the sky.



(Gareth) Okay. Is everyone ready? Okay. Okay. Five, four, three, two, one.



(Gareth) That's amazing. They all flew off really well.

(Gareth) That's such a good feeling.

(Erin) These vultures carry more than a second chance; their flight is a small victory for conservation and a quiet reminder of how fragile their place in our world truly is.

Covering over two million hectares and spanning two provinces, it’s one of the world’s biggest national parks. A critical stronghold for conservation. (Erin) But it's under siege from poachers who sometimes use deadly poisons – not bullets – to kill. (Gareth) There were just bodies everywhere. There were over a hundred dead birds in the immediate vicinity around the actual carcass. (Cell phone Subtitles) This is what the product of savagery, poisoning is. (Erin) After the discovery of what was described as a “crime scene” in the heart of the Kruger, we follow a team of dedicated conservationists fighting for the survival of a threatened species. (Jessica) So, the birds, they're falling all over the place. They're flailing; they're terrified. (Erin) It’s a story that takes us from the bush into the underbelly of the urban trade in exotic animals. (Undercover footage subtitles) I can sell you the whole vulture for R5000. (Erin) Back to the bush and a sign that all is not lost. (Gareth) Four, three, two, one. (Erin) It’s early Saturday morning, and I’m with veteran SANParks rangers Andrew and Karien Desmet. Both have spent over two decades working in the Kruger. (Erin) An elephant carcass has been discovered nearby and we're heading to the scene. (Andrew) Driving here, and we see vultures like that, we're like, “There is something here.” (Erin) Out here, death doesn't announce itself – vultures do. And they're already circling. (Andrew) What we've noticed is, as we were approaching the site, the vultures are all flying around and they're in the trees. But they're not going down onto the carcass. And that could tell us that perhaps there's a predator on the carcass. And we'll just walk slowly, listen. And then, if something happens, we're going to stand still. We're not just going to run. (Erin) It's a young elephant bull, dead a few days ago. (Erin) And definitely not poisoned? (Andrew) No. (Erin) How can you tell? (Andrew) Say we’re coming to a poisoning scene, we’d see dead flies. Then we’d know this is a poisoned carcass. (Erin) Poachers are increasingly using highly toxic agrochemical pesticides to target predators and scavengers, especially vultures. (Erin) More and more rangers in the greater Kruger National Park are finding carcasses laced with poison, and its remains like this are putting the vulture population in danger. (Erin) Last month, the park's Mahlangeni Section in northern Limpopo was the site of one of Southern Africa's deadliest wildlife poisonings. (Erin) Andrew Desmet discovered the scene from a chopper. (Andrew) There was quite a lot of the elephant that was gone. (Erin) Andrew, you were on site on the sixth of May. Can you tell us about the sequence of events for you that morning? (Andrew) We were monitoring the movement of these vultures and we saw something was developing there. And then, I think it was about half-past eight, nine o'clock at night – we just got a mortality alert on, I think, two of the tags. (Erin) The alert system, developed by the Endangered Wildlife Trust, involves fitting vultures with tags that send signals if they stop moving. (Andrew) I got airborne. I flew straight to that position. I could see dead vultures. Then I saw an elephant carcass and I can see a lot of live birds. And I could see straight away this was going to be a massive operation and I straight away started communicating with our group. (Erin) On the ground, field officer for the Endangered Wildlife Trust, Kyle Walker encountered a gruesome scene. (Erin) When does it occur to you that this is an environmental crime scene? (Kyle) Almost immediately. I do remember having to step between birds. There's birds everywhere, and you have to watch your step as you walk around, and found the next one, the next one. Each bush we were looking under, we were finding injured birds and trying to treat as quickly as possible. (Cell phone) This one has obviously died, unfortunately. (Erin) One hundred and twenty-two vultures lay dead, poisoned. They included endangered White-backed, Cape and Lappet-faced species. (Erin) Miraculously, some survived. (Kyle) Once you treat them, they do perk up a lot. So, the challenge became trying to keep the vultures with you, not letting them escape or fly off. Because they will struggle over the next few days and likely die. (Cell phone Subtitles) This one has just died. No, he’s still alive. (Erin) The clock was ticking. Saving the survivors demanded an unprecedented, coordinated effort. Over 20 personnel from conservation, veterinary and enforcement teams launched the Kruger's most extensive wildlife rescue response ever. (Jessica) A lot of them were critically ill. The poison affects the nervous system in particular. So, the birds have severely compromised breathing. (Erin) Veterinarian, Jessica Briner had to act fast. (Erin) What do you remember from when your boots were on the ground, on site? (Jessica) The numbers are in their hundreds. So, when we arrived, it was carnage because there were already so many birds deceased. There were already 123 by the time I got there. (Erin) What were you doing to help the birds? (Jessica) The main thing is to get the antidote in. The drug that we use is called Atropine. Food that is still in the crop needs to be removed, and the more fluids we can give them, the better the body can flush those poisons out. (Erin) Ninety-four vultures were either airlifted or moved by specialised ambulances for intensive care and monitoring. Gareth Tate, from The Endangered Wildlife Trust, oversaw this crucial operation. (Gareth) It really was just incredible and inspiring to see how this all came together and is testament to all the work that we've put in to get to this kind of world-class reaction unit. Our Vulture Ambulance can hold 40 birds. I think we managed to double that and even fill our canopies of our vehicles up with birds. (Cell phone Subtitles) Every single crate’s got two birds, crates scattered everywhere. (Gareth) It’s so overwhelming. Obviously, it's tragic to see those birds in pain, so it was really something. (Erin) In the past decade, populations of some vulture species have dropped by an astronomical 80%. Many are poisoned by poachers to either avoid detection or losing snared animals. Some, though, are killed for the muthi trade. (Gareth) We've seen cases of vultures, the heads and body parts removed, sometimes the entire carcass for the trade and use in traditional medicine. What we understand is that they are used for improving luck. We see it linked to gambling syndicates. So, it improves a guy’s chances of winning a gambling bet or whatever. Even individuals playing lottery are prescribed these vulture body parts, in particular the brain. (Erin) It’s ironic that consuming vultures in this way could be very unlucky. (Gareth) Often these vulture body parts are still laced with highly toxic poison, which has a human health concern. (Erin) From the scrub and savannah of the Kruger, we venture back into the city. (Erin) Joburg is home to at least two markets where the ingredients for muthi are openly sold. (Cell phone Subtitles) You can only get parts, not the whole thing. (Erin) Our team filmed undercover at two of them: the KwaMai-Mai and Faraday markets. (Cell phone Subtitles) A small piece goes for R150. (Erin) It didn't take long to find what we were looking for. (Cell phone Subtitles) I can’t give you the whole thing, just take a piece. (Erin) The body parts of a variety of vultures were on sale. We were even offered the full carcass of a critically endangered White-backed vulture. (Cell phone Subtitles) I can sell you a whole vulture for R5000. The head is R2000. (Erin) Spending a few hours in these markets reveals the extent of the challenge facing conservationists. Given the demand, it’s unlikely the mass killing in May will be the last of its kind. (Erin) But at a facility just outside Kruger, the same conservationists were preparing for the final chapter in a good news story. (Erin) At the Moholoholo Wildlife Rehab Centre in Hoedspruit, most of the rescued vultures had been treated and released. But several others, after a slower recovery, are only now ready for their return to the wild. (Nicky) And then I will put a drop in his eye. There we go. This is antibiotic eye drops. (Erin) Nicky Rappo is a veterinary nurse. (Erin) Can you tell me about what rehabilitation you've been doing with the vultures? (Nicky) When they come in, we tube them. So, we give them fluids, lots and lots of fluids. So, basically, what you want to do is flush the poison out of their system and, from there, they get better. So, you start giving them food. Once they're eating well, we can put them outside as well. (Erin) For some of Nicky’s patients, today is a big day. (Erin) In these ten crates are some of the remaining vultures from the rescue in May. But before they go into the wild, they’ll need to be fitted with tracking devices. And if some of the sounds we’ve heard are anything to go by, some of them are very ready to be set free. (Erin) Before they are released, they need to be marked and fitted with these special backpacks. (Gareth) This is the Earth Ranger software where we are able to monitor our animals, our tracked animals, at almost near-real time. We can see exactly where these birds have travelled. These provide really important insight into where these birds go and where they encounter threats in the landscape and, of course, monitor the post-rehab success. (Erin) That's it. Ten vultures in two bakkies, and we are off. (Erin) Finally, it's time for them to take to the sky. (Gareth) Okay. Is everyone ready? Okay. Okay. Five, four, three, two, one. (Gareth) That's amazing. They all flew off really well. (Gareth) That's such a good feeling. (Erin) These vultures carry more than a second chance; their flight is a small victory for conservation and a quiet reminder of how fragile their place in our world truly is.

metadata.Summary: In May 2025, Kruger National Park faced one of its gravest wildlife crises: a mass poisoning event that claimed 123 vultures, including 20 Cape Vultures—an endangered species. Poachers had laced an elephant carcass with highly toxic agrochemicals to harvest body parts for the illegal wildlife trade, leading to this devastating loss . Amidst this tragedy, a beacon of hope emerged. A rapid response team comprising SANParks rangers, the Endangered Wildlife Trust (EWT), veterinary experts, and aerial support units mobilized swiftly. Their coordinated efforts led to the rescue of 84 vultures, including Cape, White-backed, and Hooded Vultures. Utilizing emergency treatments like atropine, activated charcoal, and fluid therapy, and transporting the birds via specialized vulture ambulances and helicopters, the team achieved a remarkable 96% survival rate among the rescued birds . This incident underscores the escalating threat of poison poaching in Southern Africa, where vultures are deliberately targeted to prevent them from revealing poaching activities. The loss of these scavengers disrupts ecosystems, as vultures play a crucial role in disposing of carcasses and preventing disease spread . The successful rescue operation highlights the power of collaboration among conservationists, veterinarians, and park authorities. Carte Blanche Insert Treatment: Tonight, on Carte Blanche… In the wake of one of Southern Africa’s worst wildlife poisoning events, a coalition of conservationists, veterinarians, rangers, and pilots unite in a race against time to rescue and rehabilitate endangered vultures—highlighting the power of collaboration in combating a growing ecological crisis. Segment Overview Opening Scene: • Aerial shots of Kruger National Park's vast landscapes. • Voiceover introduces the significance of vultures in the ecosystem and the alarming rise in wildlife poisoning incidents. Act 1: The Discovery • Detail the detection of the poisoning event on May 6, 2025, by the Endangered Wildlife Trust’s (EWT) poison detection system, which monitors for unusual behavior. • First responders from SANParks and EWT arrive at the Mahlangeni Section, finding 116 vultures dead and others in distress near a poisoned elephant carcass. • Interviews with rangers and EWT officials recounting the initial response and emotional impact. Act 2: The Rescue Operation • Chronicle the rapid mobilization of individuals from various organizations, including SANParks, EWT, Moholoholo Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre, Briner Veterinary Services, and Wildscapes Veterinary Services. • Highlight the unprecedented use of SANParks helicopters to airlift 39 vultures to the SANParks K9 facility in Phalaborwa, while 45 were transported via EWT’s specialized vulture ambulance. • Behind-the-scenes footage / pictures of the rescue efforts, showcasing the coordination and urgency. ( if any are available) Act 3: Rehabilitation and Recovery • Inside look at the rehabilitation process at Moholoholo Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre, where teams worked tirelessly to stabilize and care for the vultures. • Interviews with a veterinarian discussing treatment protocols and the challenges faced. • Update on the current status of the surviving vultures, those that havee been released and plans for release back into the wild. (which we will film) Act 4: The Broader Crisis • Examination of the increasing trend of wildlife poisoning in Southern Africa, with poachers using agricultural toxins to target high-value species like vultures and lions for the illegal wildlife trade. • Discussion on the ecological impact of such poisonings and the importance of vultures in maintaining healthy ecosystems. • Insights into the collaborative efforts between SANParks, EWT, and other organizations to combat this growing threat. Closing Scene: • Footage of rehabilitated vultures being released back into the wild. • Reflections from team members on the significance of the rescue operation and the ongoing fight against wildlife poisoning. • Call to action for continued support and awareness to protect these vital scavengers and the broader ecosystem. Key Interviewees • SANParks & EWT rangers/officials involved in the initial response. • EWT officials overseeing the "Eye in the Sky" system. • Veterinarian from Moholoholo Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre, Briner Veterinary Services, and Wildscapes Veterinary Services. • Pilots who facilitated the airlifts. • Conservation experts discussing the broader implications of wildlife poisoning. ( These can be someone for EWT) Visual Elements • Drone footage of Kruger National Park and the rescue operation. • Close-up shots of vultures during rehabilitation. • illustrating the "Eye in the Sky" detection system and the spread of poisoning incidents. • Archival footage of previous wildlife poisoning events for context. Narrative Tone • Informative and urgent, emphasizing the severity of the crisis. • Hopeful and inspiring, showcasing the successful collaboration and resilience of the teams involved. • Empathetic, highlighting the emotional toll on those working to save the vultures. Objective To inform viewers about the critical issue of wildlife poisoning in Southern Africa, demonstrate the power of collaborative conservation efforts, and inspire action to protect endangered species and preserve ecological balance.
